  • G. M. Hoerzer, R. Legenstein and W. Maass. Emergence of complex computational structures from chaotic neural networks through reward-modulated Hebbian learning. Cerebral Cortex, 24(3):677–690, 2014.
  • T. Miconi. Biologically plausible learning in recurrent neural networks reproduces neural dynamics observed during cognitive tasks. eLife, 6:e20899, 2017.
  • J. Burms, K. Caluwaerts and J. Dambre. Reward-modulated Hebbian plasticity as leverage for partially embodied control in compliant robotics. Frontiers in Neurorobotics, 9:9, 2015.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the rclib User Guide. This guide will help you install the library, understand its core concepts, and build reservoir computing models for your applications.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
rclib is a C++ based Reservoir Computing library with Python bindings. It offers high performance for training large-scale Echo State Networks (ESNs) and related architectures.

Key features include:

  • Speed: Heavy lifting is done in C++ using the Eigen library.
  • Flexibility: Mix and match different reservoir types and readout algorithms.
  • Scalability: Supports large sparse reservoirs and multi-threading.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Installation: Prerequisites and installation steps.
  • Quick Start: Get up and running with a simple example.
  • Core Concepts: Learn about Reservoirs, Readouts, and Model configuration.
  • Advanced Usage: Explore Online Learning, Generative Prediction, and Parallelization.
  • Learning from Rewards: Train readouts and recurrent weights from a reward signal by exploration.

docs.title: Training on Several Sequences
docs.text:
Data often comes as several independent sequences, such as episodes or demonstrations. Concatenating them and calling fit would carry the reservoir state from the end of one sequence into the start of the next and discard the washout only once, so the readout would learn from transitions that never happen. fit_sequences treats each sequence separately: every sequence starts from reset reservoirs and drops its own first washout_len samples, and one readout is fitted on the remaining states of all sequences stacked together.

# One (n_samples, n_inputs) input array and one (n_samples, n_outputs) target
# array per episode; the lengths may differ.
inputs = [x_episode1, x_episode2, x_episode3]
targets = [y_episode1, y_episode2, y_episode3]

# Each episode warms up the reset reservoirs for 50 samples before its states count.
model.fit_sequences(inputs, targets, washout_len=50)
y_pred = model.predict(x_test)

model.fitSequences({x_episode1, x_episode2, x_episode3}, {y_episode1, y_episode2, y_episode3}, 50);

With a single sequence, fit_sequences([x], [y]) gives the same readout as fit(x, y). Pass a list even then: a single 2-D array is rejected. Every sequence must be longer than washout_len, and all sequences must have the same input width and the same target width. When retraining a model, the input width must also match the one its reservoirs were locked to by earlier input. These checks run before the model changes, and their errors name the sequence index; fit checks the locked width before it resets the reservoirs in the same way. Afterwards the reservoirs hold their states at the end of the last sequence: predict resets them first by default, while predict_online and predict_generative continue from there, so prime them with the sequence you want to continue.

docs.title: Online Learning
docs.text: For real-time applications where data arrives sequentially, use partial_fit with an RLS or LMS readout. rclib supports mini-batch updates for both, providing significant speedups when processing multiple samples at once.

docs.title: Mini-batch LMS
docs.text: The Lms readout automatically uses GEMM-based averaged batch-gradient updates when partial_fit is called with multiple samples.

docs.title: Mini-batch RLS
docs.text:
The Rls readout provides two strategies for handling mini-batches:

Solver Strategy Best For rank1_update (Default) Sequential Rank-1 updates Single samples or small batches with \(\lambda < 1.0\). rank_k_update Woodbury Rank-K update (GEMM) Mini-batches (32+) with \(\lambda = 1.0\). 
# Create an RLS readout optimized for mini-batches
readout = readouts.Rls(lambda_=1.0, delta=1.0, include_bias=True, solver="rank_k_update")
model.set_readout(readout)

# In a loop (processing 64 samples at once):
for i in range(0, len(X), 64):
    model.partial_fit(X[i : i + 64], Y[i : i + 64])

Note: rank_k_update is mathematically equivalent to sequential RLS only when the forgetting factor lambda is 1.0. For lambda < 1.0, rclib automatically falls back to sequential rank1_update to ensure mathematical correctness.

docs.title: Forgetting in RLS
docs.text:
With a forgetting factor lambda_ below 1, the default forgetting_method="exponential" forgets in every direction, also in directions that the inputs never excite. There the covariance grows as lambda_**-n and, within some multiple of 1 / (1 - lambda_) samples, the weights are lost. This is likely whenever the inputs span fewer dimensions than the readout has features: samples from one repeated trajectory, or features that are linear combinations of others. forgetting_method="directional" forgets only along each sample's input, so it keeps forgetting without winding up:

readout = readouts.Rls(lambda_=0.999, delta=1.0, include_bias=True, forgetting_method="directional")

At lambda_=1.0 the two methods are the same. Each costs one rank-1 update per sample. See Forgetting Methods.

docs.title: Generative Prediction
docs.text:
To generate sequences autonomously (feeding predictions back as inputs):

# Prime the reservoir with some initial data
prime_data = x_test[:100]
# Generate the next 200 steps
generated = model.predict_generative(prime_data, n_steps=200)
# Continue the same sequence for another 100 steps
more = model.predict_generative(np.empty((0, 1)), n_steps=100)

Every generated output, including the last, is fed back into the reservoirs, so a call with empty priming data continues where the previous call stopped: generating 200 and then 100 steps gives the same outputs and final reservoir states as generating 300 steps at once. The readout's output width must match the model's input width, since each output becomes the next input.

docs.title: Spectral Radius Scaling
docs.text:
RandomSparse draws a sparse random matrix \(\mathbf{W}_{res}\) from its seed and scales it so that its spectral radius, the largest eigenvalue modulus, equals spectral_radius. spectral_radius_method chooses how the spectral radius of the unscaled matrix is found:

Method Observed error of the scaled radius Cost Best For power_iteration (Default) Mean about 0.01%, worst 0.75% (200 seeds per size, 20 to 1000 neurons; not a bound) 1000 sparse matrix-vector products Any size dense Exact up to rounding \(O(n^3)\) time, \(O(n^2)\) memory Small reservoirs, or when the radius must be exact 
res = reservoirs.RandomSparse(n_neurons=200, spectral_radius=0.95, seed=0, spectral_radius_method="dense")

docs.title: How the default works
docs.text:
Plain power iteration multiplies a start vector by \(\mathbf{W}_{res}\) over and over, normalizing it each time, and reads the spectral radius off the norm of the last step. That converges when one real eigenvalue is clearly larger in modulus than all others, as for many symmetric matrices. The eigenvalues of a non-symmetric random matrix instead fill a disk, so the largest ones are often a complex-conjugate pair or several eigenvalues of nearly equal modulus. The iterate then keeps rotating among them and the norm of the last step oscillates instead of converging. Measured over 50 seeds at sparsity 0.1, plain power iteration with 100 steps missed the requested radius by up to 11% for 100 neurons, 6% for 300 and 4% for 1000, and more steps did not fix it.

rclib therefore averages. It runs 1000 steps from a start vector drawn from a generator seeded by seed, and returns the geometric mean of the per-step growth \(\lVert \mathbf{W}_{res} \mathbf{b}_k \rVert / \lVert \mathbf{b}_k \rVert\) over the last 500. The first 500 steps let the dominant eigenvalues take over, and averaging over many steps cancels their oscillation. Since the start vector depends only on seed, reservoirs built with the same parameters get the same weights, whatever else the program does.

The averaged estimate is still an estimate. Measured over 200 seeds for each of 20, 30, 50, 100, 300 and 1000 neurons at sparsity 0.1 and a requested radius of 0.9, the scaled matrix missed the requested radius by 0.01% to 0.02% on average. The worst seed missed by 0.75% (100 neurons); at 30 neurons, seed 113 missed by 0.47%. These figures describe that sample and are not bounds: another size, sparsity or seed can miss by more. Use spectral_radius_method="dense" when the radius must be exact.

Each step is one sparse matrix-vector product, so the cost grows with the number of non-zero weights, sparsity * n_neurons**2. Single-threaded on the development machine at sparsity 0.1, the estimate took about 0.4 ms for 100 neurons, 3 ms for 300, 27 ms for 1000 and 2 s for 10,000. The dense method took about 1.4 ms for 100 neurons, 30 ms for 300 and 1.2 s for 1000, growing as \(n^3\).

Note: rclib 0.2.0 and earlier used plain power iteration from a start vector drawn from the global std::rand() state, so only the first reservoir built in a process was reproducible. Since the averaged estimate, the same seed gives a slightly differently scaled \(\mathbf{W}_{res}\) than in those versions. Saved models keep the weights they were saved with.

docs.title: Reading the Weights
docs.text:
A trained model can be studied outside rclib, for instance by evaluating its update at states the reservoirs have never been in, to find fixed points or linearize it along a run. A RandomSparse reservoir (the object get_reservoir returns) gives copies of its weights, and a fitted ridge or RLS readout (from get_readout) its weights, for RLS as they stand after the last update, with the bias row last when it has one:

reservoir = model.get_reservoir(0)
n = reservoir.getNNeurons()
rows, cols, values = reservoir.getRecurrentWeights()  # the nonzero entries of W_res
w_res = np.zeros((n, n))
w_res[rows, cols] = values
w_in = reservoir.getInputWeights()  # (n_inputs, n); drawn at the first input, raises before it
bias = reservoir.getBias()  # (n,); zero without include_bias
leak_rate = reservoir.getLeakRate()
w_out = model.get_readout().getWeights()  # (n + 1, n_outputs) with include_bias=True


def advance(state, u):
    """The state after the input u, as the reservoir computes it."""
    return (1 - leak_rate) * state + leak_rate * np.tanh(u @ w_in + bias + state @ w_res)


state = advance(reservoir.getState(), u)
y = state @ w_out[:-1] + w_out[-1]  # model.predict_online(u) for a single reservoir

States and inputs are row vectors, so the entry (i, j) of W_res is the weight from neuron i to neuron j. W_res comes as its nonzero entries, so that a large reservoir need not be made dense; scipy.sparse.coo_array((values, (rows, cols)), shape=(n, n)) builds the sparse matrix.

docs.title: Ridge Regression Solver Selection
docs.text:
rclib provides multiple strategies for batch training. While the auto mode is recommended, you can explicitly set the solver based on your specific needs.

# Create a Ridge readout with an explicit solver
# Available: "auto", "cholesky", "dual_cholesky",
#            "conjugate_gradient", "conjugate_gradient_implicit"
readout = readouts.Ridge(alpha=1e-8, include_bias=True, solver="dual_cholesky")
Solver Best For cholesky Small reservoirs or when \(N \le T\). dual_cholesky Large reservoirs with fewer samples (\(N > T\)). conjugate_gradient_implicit Extremely large reservoirs (n_features >= 4,000). auto (Default) Automatically chooses the most efficient strategy.

docs.title: Next-Generation RC (NVAR)
docs.text:
rclib supports NVAR, which uses time-delayed polynomial features instead of a random network. polynomial_order=1 is a linear delay embedding; higher orders append all monomials with replacement up to that degree.

res = reservoirs.Nvar(num_lags=5, polynomial_order=2)
# ... use as a normal reservoir

docs.title: Saving and Loading Models
docs.text:
A model can be written to a file and restored later, from Python or from C++. Files are interchangeable between the two, because both go through the same C++ code.

from rclib import ESN

model.fit(x_train, y_train, washout_len=100)
model.save("mackey_glass.rclib")

restored = ESN.load("mackey_glass.rclib")
y_pred = restored.predict(x_test)

model.save("mackey_glass.rclib");
Model restored = Model::load("mackey_glass.rclib");

The file holds the configuration, the trained weights (the random reservoir matrices themselves, not just their seed), the RLS/LMS training state and the current reservoir states. A restored model therefore continues where the original stopped: predict_online, partial_fit, and predict_generative without priming data all behave as they would have on the original. ESN objects also support pickle and copy.deepcopy, which use the same format.

Saving replaces an existing file in one step: if saving fails, the existing file is left unchanged. Every save or load failure raises rclib.SerializationError (a RuntimeError subclass; SerializationError in C++). Examples are a model without a reservoir, a component whose widths do not match its neighbours, a custom reservoir or readout type, the same reservoir object added twice (C++ only), and a corrupted or truncated file. Running out of memory raises MemoryError (std::bad_alloc in C++) instead.

Compatibility: Files written by rclib 0.2.0 still load; their RandomSparse reservoirs report spectral_radius_method="power_iteration". Files of model format version 1 or 2 load with bias_scaling=1.0. Files written by later versions use model format version 4, which adds reward-modulated components and models without a readout, and cannot be read by rclib 0.2.0 or by builds that write an earlier version.

Security: Only load files from sources you trust. Unlike pickle, the format contains no executable code, but it is parsed by native code. Loading a pickled ESN is as unsafe as any other unpickling.

Portability: On the same build and settings, a restored model produces bit-identical results. Files load on every supported (little-endian) platform and the stored values are exact, but computations on a different compiler, CPU or thread configuration can round differently, and nothing bounds how far such differences grow: recurrent updates, generative rollouts and continued training can amplify them. A RandomSparse reservoir that has never received input has no input weights yet; they are generated from the seed on first use and can differ across platforms, so fit the model before saving if you need portable weights.

docs.title: Parallelization Configuration
docs.text:
You can optimize performance for your hardware by configuring CMake options during the build.

Option Default Best For RCLIB_USE_OPENMP ON Multi-core CPUs RCLIB_ENABLE_EIGEN_PARALLELIZATION ON Balanced performance (Default) RCLIB_ADAPTIVE_PARALLELIZATION ON Automatic switching based on problem size (N > 1000)

docs.title: Common Scenarios
docs.text:
1. Default (Adaptive) Automatically uses serial mode for small reservoirs to avoid overhead and parallel mode for large ones. 

CMAKE_ARGS="-DRCLIB_ADAPTIVE_PARALLELIZATION=ON" uv sync

2. Forced Parallelism Force parallel execution even for small reservoirs. 

CMAKE_ARGS="-DRCLIB_ADAPTIVE_PARALLELIZATION=OFF" uv sync

3. Completely Serial Disable all multi-threading (best for debugging). 

CMAKE_ARGS="-DRCLIB_USE_OPENMP=OFF" uv sync

docs.title: Configuring Reservoirs
docs.text:
The reservoir is the dynamical core of the ESN. rclib provides RandomSparse for standard ESNs.

res = reservoirs.RandomSparse(
    n_neurons=1000,  # Size of the reservoir
    spectral_radius=0.9,  # Scaling of spectral radius
    sparsity=0.1,  # Density of connections
    leak_rate=1.0,  # 1.0 = full update, < 1.0 = leaky integrator
    input_scaling=1.0,  # Scaling of input weights
    include_bias=False,  # Add a random bias to each neuron
    seed=42,  # Random seed for reproducibility
    spectral_radius_method="power_iteration",  # or "dense": exact, O(n^3) time, small reservoirs only
    bias_scaling=1.0,  # Range of the bias, [-bias_scaling, bias_scaling]
)

With include_bias=True, each neuron receives a constant bias drawn uniformly from \([-1, 1]\) and multiplied by bias_scaling, which sets the bias's range apart from input_scaling. The draws do not depend on bias_scaling: the same seed gives the same recurrent and input weights at every bias_scaling, and the default of 1 gives the unscaled bias.

spectral_radius_method chooses how the spectral radius of the random weight matrix is found before the matrix is scaled to spectral_radius. The default "power_iteration" estimates it. In measurements the scaled radius was usually within about 0.01% of the request and at worst 0.75% off, but these are observations, not bounds. "dense" is exact but costs \(O(n^3)\) time and \(O(n^2)\) memory in n_neurons, so use it for small reservoirs or when the radius must be exact. See Spectral Radius Scaling.

docs.title: Configuring Readouts
docs.text:
The readout maps the high-dimensional reservoir state to the target output.

  • Ridge Regression (readouts.Ridge): The standard offline training method. Fast and stable.
  • Recursive Least Squares (readouts.Rls): For online, adaptive learning. With a forgetting factor below 1, forgetting_method="directional" keeps it from winding up when the inputs excite only some directions (see Forgetting in RLS).
  • Least Mean Squares (readouts.Lms): A simpler gradient-based online method.

Ridge readouts regularize all fitted weights, including the appended constant feature when include_bias=True.

docs.title: Building the Model
docs.text:
The ESN class acts as a container.

model = ESN(connection_type="serial")  # "serial" or "parallel"
model.add_reservoir(res1)
# For deep ESNs:
# model.add_reservoir(res2)
model.set_readout(readout)

docs.title: Training
docs.text: model.fit(x, y, washout_len=k) resets the reservoirs, runs them through the whole input sequence and fits the readout on all but the first k states. For several independent sequences, such as episodes, use model.fit_sequences([x1, x2], [y1, y2], washout_len=k): each sequence starts from reset reservoirs and loses its own washout before one readout is fitted on all of them. See Training on Several Sequences.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Operating System: Linux (the only platform tested and supported).
  • C++ Compiler: Must support C++17 (e.g., GCC 9+, Clang 10+).
  • CMake: Version 3.15 or higher.
  • Python: Version 3.11 or higher.
  • OpenMP: Required for parallelization.
    • Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install libomp-dev

docs.title: Installing with uv (Recommended)
docs.text:
The recommended way to install and manage rclib for development is using uv.

# Clone the repository
git clone --recursive https://github.com/hrshtst/rclib.git
cd rclib

# Install dependencies and the project (wraps the required two-step `uv sync`)
./scripts/setup-dev.sh

docs.title: Installing via pip
docs.text:
You can also install it using standard pip:

pip install .

Note: The --recursive flag in git clone is crucial because rclib uses submodules for its C++ dependencies (Eigen, Catch2, pybind11).

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Here is a minimal example to train an ESN on a simple sine wave task.

import numpy as np
from rclib import ESN, readouts, reservoirs

# 1. Prepare data
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 1000).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.sin(x)

# Split into train/test
train_len = 800
x_train, y_train = x[:train_len], y[:train_len]
x_test, y_test = x[train_len:], y[train_len:]

# 2. Configure Reservoir
res = reservoirs.RandomSparse(n_neurons=500, spectral_radius=0.9, sparsity=0.1, leak_rate=0.5, seed=42)

# 3. Configure Readout (Ridge Regression)
readout = readouts.Ridge(alpha=1e-6, include_bias=True)

# 4. Build Model
model = ESN()
model.add_reservoir(res)
model.set_readout(readout)

# 5. Train
model.fit(x_train, y_train, washout_len=50)

# 6. Predict
y_pred = model.predict(x_test)

# Calculate error
mse = np.mean((y_pred - y_test) ** 2)
print(f"Test MSE: {mse:.4e}")

docs.title: Learning from Rewards
docs.text: Supervised readouts learn from targets. A reward-modulated model learns from a scalar reward instead: it explores by perturbing its own activity, and correlates the perturbations with the reward it receives. This suits goal-directed tasks where no target output is known, only how good the behaviour was: control, decision making, and closed loops with an environment or a body. The theory page explains the rule and why it works.

docs.title: The Closed Loop
docs.text:
A reward-modulated model is driven with two calls:

  • ESN.act(x) steps the model through the input rows, adds exploration noise and records each step's eligibility, and returns the outputs.
  • ESN.reinforce(reward) changes the weights in proportion to the eligibility and to how the reward compares with the reward expected so far.
import numpy as np
from rclib import ESN, learning, readouts, reservoirs

rule = learning.hoerzer2014(5e-3, learning_rate_decay_steps=10_000.0)
esn = ESN()
esn.add_reservoir(reservoirs.RandomSparse(n_neurons=300, spectral_radius=1.2, leak_rate=0.1, seed=0))
esn.set_readout(readouts.RewardModulated(1, rule, include_bias=False))

output = np.zeros((1, 1))
for step in range(100_000):
    output = esn.act(output)  # the noisy output is fed back as the next input
    target = 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * step / 100)
    esn.reinforce(-float((output[0, 0] - target) ** 2))

The readout never sees the target: it only learns whether each step's error beat its recent average. Afterwards esn.predict_generative(np.empty((0, 1)), 500) generates the sine on its own, without noise.

docs.title: Building Blocks
docs.text:
The rule. learning.RewardModulatedHebbian holds every setting, grouped with learning.Exploration (the noise) and learning.Baseline (the expected reward). It is a frozen dataclass: build it with keywords and copy it with dataclasses.replace.

rule = learning.RewardModulatedHebbian(
    learning_rate=0.05,
    exploration=learning.Exploration(distribution="uniform", amplitude=0.2, seed=1),
    post="high_pass",  # the potential minus its recent average estimates the noise
    update="online",  # update at every reward
    modulator="difference",  # R - R_avg
    baseline=learning.Baseline(kind="ema", decay=0.8),
)

The presets learning.legenstein2010, learning.hoerzer2014, learning.miconi2017 and learning.burms2015 set the choices of four published variants and take the learning rate and any setting to override. They are starting points: the learning rate and the exploration amplitude depend on the task.

Where it learns.

  • readouts.RewardModulated(n_outputs, rule, include_bias=...) is a linear readout whose output gets the exploration noise. Its weights start at zero at the first act; esn.get_readout().setWeights(W) sets them first.
  • reservoirs.RewardModulated(n_neurons, spectral_radius, ..., rule=rule) is a random sparse reservoir whose recurrent weights learn. Its neurons integrate a potential with the leak rate and fire at its tanh, so a perturbation lingers for about 1 / leak_rate steps. plastic_presynaptic and plastic_postsynaptic list the neurons whose synapses learn; the others keep their weights.

A model can hold reward-modulated reservoirs, a reward-modulated readout, or both: reinforce updates all of them, each with its own baseline.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
A reward every step. Call act with one row and reinforce after it, with an online rule such as legenstein2010 or hoerzer2014.

One reward per trial. Use a trial rule (update="trial", as in miconi2017 and burms2015): act through the whole trial, then reinforce once. The eligibility sums the trial and the update clears it. Pass the trial type as key so that each type has its own baseline:

esn.reset_reservoirs()  # each trial from rest
rates = esn.act(trial_inputs)  # one call for the whole trial
esn.reinforce(-error, key=trial_type)

Output feedback. Append the output to the next input: the input weights drawn for those columns act as feedback weights, uniform in [-input_scaling, input_scaling] times the factor you scale the output by. With the output as the only input, predict_generative runs the noise-free closed loop.

Learning from observations. reservoirs.Nvar(num_lags=1, polynomial_order=1) passes its input through unchanged, so a reward-modulated readout learns directly from observations, for example the sensors of a robot or a simulated body that plays the role of the reservoir.

Outputs from the reservoir. A model without a readout returns the reservoir's rates from act, so designated neurons can be the outputs while the recurrent weights learn. Exclude them from the plastic lists to keep their synapses fixed.

Your own critic. reinforce(reward, baseline=b) compares the reward with b instead of the internal baseline, which is then left unchanged; modulate(m) applies a modulator directly, for example a temporal-difference error.

Supervised start, reward fine-tuning. Fit a Ridge readout, read its weights, then switch to a reward-modulated readout that starts from them:

weights = esn.get_readout().getWeights()
esn.set_readout(readouts.RewardModulated(n_outputs, rule, include_bias=True))
esn.get_readout().setWeights(weights)

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• act(x, explore=False) is a noise-free step that changes no learning state; with a readout it equals predict_online. predict and predict_generative are noise-free too. Before a reward-modulated readout's weights exist, a noise-free step outputs zeros.
  • An exploration amplitude of 0 removes the noise but does not stop every rule: with a "high_pass" or "potential" post signal the weights still change when the inputs change. Use explore=False to step without recording eligibility.
  • reinforce needs an exploring act since the previous update; otherwise it raises RuntimeError and changes nothing.
  • The first reward of a key with an "ema" or "window" baseline becomes its own baseline, so it changes no weights; the update still counts toward learning_rate_decay_steps.
  • reset_reservoirs() resets the activity, including the averages the high-pass signal uses, but keeps the eligibility. clear_eligibility() drops it, for example after an aborted trial.
  • Updates apply to all reward-modulated components or to none: a non-finite reward raises ValueError, and a row or update that would overflow raises RuntimeError, in each case without changing any weights, eligibility or baselines.
  • A reservoir object may appear only once in a model that acts.
  • fit and partial_fit do not apply to a reward-modulated readout.
  • The model file format stores the rule and the whole learning state, including the noise generator, so a model saved, pickled or copied in the middle of learning continues exactly. A model without a readout can be saved too.
  • get_readout().getLearning() and get_reservoir(i).getLearning() give read-only access to the eligibility, baselines and update count.

docs.text:
Each example in examples/python/ distills one paper's main claim at a small scale; its outcome is a property of that demonstration, not a reproduction of the paper.
